*Figures below are drawn from `qmd_reports/report_nedlame_treatment_comparison.qmd`, which has the full methodology, caveats, and charts. This is a summary for discussion, not a standalone analysis — if the full report changes, this page needs to be regenerated to match.*

## The pilot, in brief

718 cows have received a Nedap mobility-alert (`NEDLAME`) over a ~9-week window (2026-06-02 to 2026-08-03) — the alert system's history to date. Of those, **81 are excluded from the TX-vs-Control comparisons below** (see "New this round" — their alert almost certainly reflects a post-trim gait change, not an independent catch), leaving an analysis cohort of **637**: **278 automatically trimmed (TX)** and **359 left to staff's judgment (Control)**. Every finding below is an early read on a still-young pilot — not a mature-study conclusion.

## New this round: a real, quantified data-quality finding

A close read of one case (cow 7207) turned up a broader pattern: **`NEDLAME`'s daily batch import stamps each alert with the day it was *loaded* (~5am), not necessarily the day the underlying sensor event happened** — and trim records are commonly entered a day or two late (correctly backdated, but not yet in the system when the next alert batch runs). The result: some alerts that fire 1-7 days *after* a trim aren't the camera making an independent catch — they're the camera picking up that cow's own post-treatment soreness/altered gait.

This turned out to be real and sizeable, not a one-off: **122 of 957 total `NEDLAME` events (12.8%) fire within 14 days after a trim**, almost all genuine decline signals rather than noise, and **81 of the 718 pilot cows had their very first alert fire this way** — of those, **80 showed a real decline signal, and the large majority never had any further lameness event of any kind afterward**, strong evidence nothing was actually wrong. Per Gerard's direction, these 81 cows (43 Control / 38 TX) are now excluded from the main cohort and reported separately in a new "Excluded" section, rather than silently counted as ordinary detections. **Checked separately: this pattern does *not* affect Q4's "did NEDAP catch it" numbers below** — those draw from the whole herd's alert history directly, not from this cohort.

## Headline findings

1. **Milk production**: no clear separation between arms, and the two arms now track *closer* together than before the exclusion — TX 93.9% of baseline by day 30 vs. Control 93.4% (previously TX looked slightly worse, at 92.4% vs. 93.8%). Consistent with the excluded cows never having had a real lameness-driven milk impact to begin with.

2. **Time to next trim/lameness event**: with the artifact cases removed, the gap between arms is even more pronounced than before — TX reaches a subsequent trim/LAME event in 83.9% of cases within 30 days vs. 28.2% for Control (up from 76.2%/28.2% pre-exclusion, since the excluded cows were disproportionately "nothing ever happened" cases). **About half of TX's first follow-up visits still find nothing** (55.0% trim-only/no lesion, vs. 41.4% for Control) — the over-trimming rate itself is essentially unchanged by the exclusion.

3. **Independent staff detection**: staff catch lame cows on their own at a similar rate regardless of arm (Control 18.7%, TX 20.5%, both up slightly post-exclusion) — the alert + auto-trim protocol isn't replacing staff vigilance, it's running alongside it. Staff catch `Strong Decline` alerts meaningfully more often than `Low Decline` ones, and that gap widened for TX specifically this round (34.6% vs. 15.8%, up from 29.7%/14.9%).

4. **What NEDAP is missing** *(unaffected by this round's exclusion — drawn from the whole herd, not the cohort above)*: across the whole herd, **67.2% of lesion diagnoses since June 1 weren't caught by a NEDLAME alert first** (cases too recently trimmed/diagnosed or already dried off are excluded from this count entirely, since NEDAP can't structurally alert in either situation). The majority of that gap is cows who were **never alerted at all** (219 of 418 qualifying cases, 52%). Among cows who *were* eventually alerted, TX's arm closes the gap faster (20.2% missed vs. 44.4% for Control). **Staff aren't fully backstopping those misses either**: of 281 cases NEDAP missed, only 67 (23.8%) had a farm staff check (`CHKLAME`) in the week before diagnosis.

   A raw Nedap sensor export separates a *true* sensor miss from a case where the sensor fired but the flag never reached DairyComp. For the window that export covers (2025-08-25 to 2026-07-16), of the **214** DC-recorded misses inside it, **71 (33.2%) actually had the sensor fire in time** — a pipeline/integration gap, not a detection failure — leaving **143** true misses at the sensor level. **Roughly a third of what looks like a NEDAP miss in DairyComp is really a data-pipeline problem, not a sensor problem**, at least in the checkable window. (104 more recent lesion cases fall after the export's coverage ends and can't be checked yet.)

5. **Lameness history**: 42.4% of the cohort (270 of 637) carry a `Chronic` history label — essentially unchanged from before the exclusion, and still mostly an artifact of how chronicity is defined (any 2nd+ diagnosis more than a day apart) rather than evidence of active, recurring problems. Still only 3 cows total with a `Repeat` history label.

6. **Culling**: 19 of 359 Control cows (5.3%) and 13 of 278 TX cows (4.7%) have been culled so far — close enough, and early enough, that this shouldn't be read as a treatment effect yet.

## What this suggests for discussion

- **Two real, independent pipeline/data-quality issues are now quantified this round** — a sensor→DairyComp integration gap (finding 4, ~33% of checkable misses) and a batch-load-timing artifact that inflates the apparent alert count by ~11% of the cohort (the exclusion above). Neither is a detection-algorithm problem; both are fixable process/integration issues, and both are worth raising with the Nedap/DairyComp integration team ahead of tuning anything about the sensor's actual sensitivity.
- The auto-trim protocol gets cows seen faster, at the cost of trimming a lot of cows who turn out fine — that trade-off looks *slightly worse* after cleaning out the artifact cases (TX's "found nothing" rate held steady at 55% while its "any event" rate climbed), worth weighing against the labor/hoof-health cost.
- Staff are already catching a meaningful share of lame cows on their own, alert or no alert — the pilot's main value-add may be less about replacing staff judgment and more about the cows staff *aren't* catching.
- The single biggest gap in DairyComp's own record is cows who never get alerted in the first place, not cows who get alerted too late — and with a third of that gap now known to be pipeline loss rather than true detection failure, the real "sensor truly never fired" rate is likely smaller than 52% once the sensor-side check is extended to the full period.
- Everything here is based on ~9 weeks of `NEDLAME` history. Time-to-event and culling findings especially will keep firming up with more data — worth revisiting this summary again once there's a few more months on the clock, and once a fresher raw sensor export closes the current coverage gap.
